verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of Songs and the First Longing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's (v. 1). The bride longs for her beloved: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine (v. 2). His name is like poured-out oil (v. 3). Draw me after you; let us run, and the king brings her into his chambers, while others rejoice with them (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The Bible's great love song opens with desire that is honest, joyful and directed to one beloved.

verseByVerse.quote: The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's.

The title tells us what kind of book this is and how highly it is to be valued. The Song of Songs is built like "King of kings" or "holy of holies": the finest of songs, the song above all songs. Solomon, Scripture says, wrote many: He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005 (1 Kgs 4:32). Of all of them, this is the one given the title.

And it is a love song. There is no other book in the Bible like it. No law, no history, no prophecy, and God is named only once, near the end, in the very flame of the LORD (8:6). It is a poem of desire and delight between a man and a woman, full of gardens, vineyards, perfume and longing. The ESV prints labels over the speeches (She, He, Others), and its footnote says honestly that these are the translators' additions, based on whether the Hebrew words are masculine or feminine, singular or plural.

How should a Christian read it? First, as what it plainly is: a celebration of love between husband and wife. God made man and woman, and he made them for each other: Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed (Gen 2:24-25). The Song is that verse set to music. Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled (Heb 13:4). A church that is embarrassed by this book has become more prudish than God.

Second, because Scripture itself says that marriage is a picture of something greater, the Song also lifts our eyes. Paul quotes Genesis 2 and adds, This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church (Eph 5:32). Every true marriage is a small echo of the love of Christ for his bride. So the Song is not a code in which every detail stands for a doctrine. It is a love song about marriage that, read in the light of the whole Bible, makes the heart long for the love of which all marriage is a picture.

verseByVerse.quote: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine; your anointing oils are fragrant; your name is oil poured out; therefore virgins love you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine;

The Song begins in the middle of desire. No introduction, no scene-setting: a woman longing to be kissed. And it is the woman who speaks first. In a book from Solomon's world, which often treated women as property, the Bible's love song opens with a woman's voice and a woman's longing, spoken without shame.

Notice the change of person. Let him kiss me, and then your love. She begins speaking about him and ends speaking to him, the way love does when the beloved comes near. And his love is better than wine: sweeter, more gladdening, more intoxicating than the best the table can offer.

your anointing oils are fragrant; your name is oil poured out; therefore virgins love you.

His fragrance fills the room, and so does his name. A person's name in Scripture is his character and reputation. His is like perfumed oil poured out: it spreads, and everyone who comes near it is drawn. She is not the only one who admires him; virgins love you. He is worthy of love, and she knows it.

A believer reading these lines can hardly help thinking of the one whom Psalm 45 describes: You are the most handsome of the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips (Ps 45:2). The love of Christ is better than wine. And the order of the Song is the order of the gospel: we are drawn to him because his love came first. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Draw me after you; let us run. The king has brought me into his chambers. We will exult and rejoice in you; we will extol your love more than wine; rightly do they love you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Draw me after you; let us run. The king has brought me into his chambers.

Draw me: she wants him to lead, and she wants to follow eagerly, let us run. Love is not reluctant. And the king does bring her in, into his private rooms, the place of intimacy. He is called the king, and throughout the Song the bridegroom is spoken of in royal terms. To the woman who loves him, her husband is a king.

We will exult and rejoice in you; we will extol your love more than wine; rightly do they love you.

Now others join in: We will exult and rejoice in you. Love between a husband and wife is private, and it is also something the community celebrates. Every wedding feast says so. And the chorus agrees with the bride: rightly do they love you. He deserves it.

For the Christian, the prayer Draw me after you; let us run is the prayer of every heart that has tasted the love of Christ. We do not come to him on our own; Jesus said that no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). But when he draws, we run. When did you last run to him, rather than drag your feet?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I am very dark, but lovely: the sun has darkened her while her brothers made her work the vineyards, and her own vineyard she has not kept (vv. 5-6). She asks where her beloved pastures his flock (v. 7), and is told to follow the tracks of the flock to the shepherds' tents (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Love sees and delights in the one who feels unseen and unlovely.

verseByVerse.quote: I am very dark, but lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon. Do not gaze at me because I am dark, because the sun has looked upon me. My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am very dark, but lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.

The bride turns to the women of the city, and her words carry both embarrassment and confidence. I am very dark, but lovely. The tents of Kedar were the black goat-hair tents of desert nomads; the curtains of Solomon were rich royal hangings. She is dark like the one, and lovely like the other.

Do not gaze at me because I am dark, because the sun has looked upon me. My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept!

She explains. Her skin has been darkened by the sun, because she has been working outdoors. Her brothers were angry with her and sent her to labour in the vineyards. In a court where beauty meant pale, pampered skin, she looks like a field worker, and she feels it. Do not gaze at me. And she has had no time to care for herself: my own vineyard I have not kept.

Many people know that feeling. The mother who has given years to others and feels she has let herself go. The person who has been shamed by family and carries it into every room. She stands before the fashionable women of Jerusalem and wants to hide.

But she also says but lovely, and the rest of the chapter shows why she can say it: her beloved thinks so. Love does not wait for us to become beautiful before it delights in us. The love of Christ is like that. He did not love a church that was already spotless; he loved her so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27). His love makes lovely.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture your flock, where you make it lie down at noon; for why should I be like one who veils herself beside the flocks of your companions? If you do not know, O most beautiful among women, follow in the tracks of the flock, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds' tents.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture your flock, where you make it lie down at noon; for why should I be like one who veils herself beside the flocks of your companions?

You whom my soul loves: the phrase will return again and again (3:1-4). Her beloved is pictured as a shepherd, and she wants to know where to find him at midday rest. She does not want to wander among the other shepherds' flocks like a veiled woman looking for company, a figure who might be mistaken for someone of doubtful reputation. She wants him, and only him.

If you do not know, O most beautiful among women, follow in the tracks of the flock, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds' tents.

The answer comes lightly, perhaps teasingly: if you do not know, follow the tracks of the flock. And it calls her most beautiful among women, the very woman who had just asked not to be gazed at.

The picture of the shepherd who makes his flock lie down at noon is familiar from the Psalms: He makes me lie down in green pastures (Ps 23:2). And Jesus said, I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14). The soul that loves him wants to know where he is, and the way to find him is still to follow in the tracks of the flock, among his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Beautiful in Each Other's Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He compares her to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots and praises her adornment (vv. 9-11). She speaks of him as a fragrance close to her heart (vv. 12-14). Behold, you are beautiful, my love, he says; Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, she answers, and their meeting place is green, with beams of cedar and rafters of pine (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Married love is a delight each gives the other in words as well as in presence.

verseByVerse.quote: I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots. Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments, your neck with strings of jewels. We will make for you ornaments of gold, studded with silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots.

Now he speaks, and his first words are praise. To modern ears a comparison to a horse may sound odd, but in Solomon's world the horses of Pharaoh's chariots were prized animals, beautifully harnessed and adorned. She stands out like that. She said, Do not gaze at me. He cannot help it.

Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments, your neck with strings of jewels. We will make for you ornaments of gold, studded with silver.

He notices details: her cheeks, her neck, her jewellery. Love pays attention. And the ESV notes that the you in verse 11 is feminine singular: the gift of gold and silver is for her. She came feeling like a field hand; she is treated like a queen.

Husbands, notice what the bridegroom does. He speaks his admiration aloud, specifically, and he gives. Many wives have not heard specific words of delight from their husbands in years. The Song teaches men to say them.

verseByVerse.quote: While the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance. My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh that lies between my breasts. My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of Engedi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance.

She answers with fragrance. Nard was a costly perfume from far away. While the king reclined, her perfume filled the room: her love for him is like that, spreading to where he is.

My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh that lies between my breasts. My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of Engedi.

A small bag of myrrh worn at the breast keeps its scent close all day and night. So is he to her: close to her heart, never out of her awareness. And like a cluster of henna flowers in the oasis of Engedi, a green place of springs in the desert by the Dead Sea, he is refreshment in a dry land.

Twice she says My beloved is to me. Not what he is to others, but what he is to her. That is how love speaks. And it is how faith speaks of Christ: not only that he is lovely, but that he is lovely to me, the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Gal 2:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you are beautiful, my love; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves. Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, truly delightful. Our couch is green; the beams of our house are cedar; our rafters are pine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, you are beautiful, my love; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves.

He says it twice. You are beautiful. The woman who did not want to be looked at is told, again, that she is beautiful. Her eyes are like doves: gentle, soft, perhaps quick and bright. Love repeats itself, because the heart that is loved needs to hear it more than once.

Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, truly delightful. Our couch is green; the beams of our house are cedar; our rafters are pine.

And she says it back. The same words, returned: you are beautiful, my beloved. Their love is mutual, each delighting in the other. Then she looks around their meeting place. It seems to be outdoors: the couch is the green grass, the beams and rafters are the branches of cedar and pine overhead. The whole world has become their house.

Here is a picture of marriage as God meant it: two people who look at each other and say, you are beautiful, and mean it, and find that wherever they are together is home. That love has to be tended, and much of the rest of the Song will show how. But it begins here, in delight given and returned.

1.title: The Song of Songs: Let Him Kiss Me
1.overview:
The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's (v. 1) is the finest of songs, a love poem between a bride and her bridegroom. The ESV's speaker labels are the translators' additions. The bride longs for her beloved's kisses, declares his love better than wine, and asks him to draw her after him; the king brings her into his chambers, and others rejoice with them (vv. 2-4).

She is self-conscious before the daughters of Jerusalem, dark from working in her brothers' vineyards and without time to care for herself, yet she says she is lovely (vv. 5-6). She asks where her shepherd pastures his flock and is told to follow the flock's tracks (vv. 7-8).

He praises her beauty and promises her ornaments of gold (vv. 9-11). She speaks of him as a sachet of myrrh close to her heart (vv. 12-14). Each tells the other, you are beautiful, and their green meeting place becomes their home (vv. 15-17).
1.theology:
God created marriage and the delight of husband and wife, and the Song celebrates that gift without shame (Gen 2:24-25; Heb 13:4). Desire within marriage is good, mutual and to be spoken (vv. 2, 15-16).

Marriage is a picture of Christ and the church (Eph 5:31-32). Read in that light, the Song shows love that comes first and draws the beloved (v. 4; 1 John 4:19), and love that delights in one who feels unlovely and makes her lovely (vv. 5-6, 15; Eph 5:27).
1.examples:
A woman's voice speaking first, and without shame.

The mother who feels she has let herself go.

A sachet of myrrh worn close to the heart all day.

A husband who has not said a specific word of admiration in years.

A couch of green grass under cedar branches.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — His Banner over Me Was Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She calls herself a simple wildflower, and he calls her a lily among brambles (vv. 1-2). She delights in his shade and fruit (v. 3). He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love (v. 4). She is faint with love, held in his embrace (vv. 5-6), and charges the daughters of Jerusalem that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Love protects and displays the beloved, and it must be kept for its proper time.

verseByVerse.quote: I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys. As a lily among brambles, so is my love among the young women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys.

Hymns have often sung these words about Christ, but in the Song it is the bride who says them, about herself. And she is not boasting. The ESV notes that the flower meant is probably a bulb, "such as a crocus, asphodel, or narcissus", the ordinary wildflowers that covered the coastal plain of Sharon in spring. She is saying, I am just one flower among thousands in the field.

As a lily among brambles, so is my love among the young women.

He takes her modest words and turns them around. Yes, a lily, but a lily among brambles. To him every other woman is a thorn bush, and she is the one flower. She says, I am ordinary. He says, you are the only one.

That is what love does to a person who thinks little of herself. It does not argue her into self-esteem. It simply sees her differently and says so. And it is how Christ sees his people: not as one more face in the crowd, but as his own, known by name.

verseByVerse.quote: As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the young men. With great delight I sat in his shadow, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the young men.

She answers with a matching picture. Among the forest trees, which give shade but no food, he is an apple tree: shade and fruit together. Every other man is ordinary timber; he is the one who nourishes.

With great delight I sat in his shadow, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.

Two gifts of the apple tree: shade from the heat, and sweet fruit. She rests in his protection and enjoys what he gives. A good husband is both: a shelter his wife can rest under, and a source of delight.

The believer knows this double gift in Christ. His shadow is refuge; his fruit is sweet. Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him! (Ps 34:8).

verseByVerse.quote: He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love. Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am sick with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.

The ESV notes that the banqueting house is in Hebrew "the house of wine": the place of feasting and celebration. He brings her in, and over her flies his banner. A banner marked where an army belonged and whose they were. His banner over her, the flag that says to everyone whose she is, is love.

What a thing for a woman to be able to say about her husband: when he brings me into company, everyone can see that he loves me. He is not ashamed of her; he displays his love.

And the church can say it of Christ. He has brought us to his table, and the banner over us is not our record or our achievements, but his love. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8).

Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am sick with love.

She is faint, overwhelmed, sick with love, and asks for raisin cakes and apples to revive her. Anyone who has been deeply in love knows the lightheadedness. The Song does not treat that as silly. It is part of the gift.

verseByVerse.quote: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me! I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me!

The picture is of lovers lying together, his left arm cradling her head, his right arm around her. It is tender and intimate, and the Song does not blush at it. This is the embrace of marriage, and God calls it good.

I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.

And immediately a warning. The ESV notes that I adjure you means "I put you on oath", and that the phrase is used throughout the Song. This charge will be repeated twice more (3:5; 8:4). Having described the delight of love's embrace, the bride turns to the unmarried young women and puts them under oath: do not awaken this before its time.

Sexual love is like a fire. In the hearth of marriage it warms a home; set loose too early, it burns the house down. Do not stir it up by what you watch, what you read, how you touch, where you let your imagination go, before the time God has made for it. For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor (1 Thess 4:3-4).

This is not a word only for teenagers. It is a word for the married person tempted to awaken desire for someone who is not his spouse. Love has its time and its place, and guarding it is part of loving well.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — Arise, My Love, and Come Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping over the hills, and stands gazing through the lattice (vv. 8-9). Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away, for behold, the winter is past (vv. 10-13). He longs to see her face and hear her voice (v. 14), and asks that the little foxes be caught (v. 15). My beloved is mine, and I am his (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The beloved comes and calls; love answers, guards what is precious, and rests in mutual belonging.

verseByVerse.quote: The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills. My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Behold, there he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, looking through the lattice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.

A new scene. She hears his voice before she sees him, and her heart leaps. He is coming, and nothing slows him down: mountains and hills are nothing to him. Love finds a way.

My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Behold, there he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, looking through the lattice.

Swift and strong like a young stag, he arrives at her house and stands outside, looking in through the window lattice. He wants to see her. He will not force the door; he calls.

That is a lovely picture of how Christ comes to his people. He does not break down doors. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Rev 3:20).

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved speaks and says to me: "Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away, for behold, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. The fig tree ripens its figs, and the vines are in blossom; they give forth fragrance. Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My beloved speaks and says to me: "Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away, for behold, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone.

His invitation is one of the most beautiful passages in the book. Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away. Come out of the house; come with me. And the reason is spring. In Israel the winter is the season of cold rains; now it is over.

The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. The fig tree ripens its figs, and the vines are in blossom; they give forth fragrance. Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.

Everything is coming to life: flowers, birdsong, figs, vine blossom. The ESV notes that singing may be rendered "pruning", the season when vines are cut back for growth. Either way, the world is new, and he wants to enjoy it with her. And he ends as he began: Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.

Marriages go through winters: seasons of grief, illness, distance, dullness. This passage is a call to notice when spring comes, and to go out together into it. When did you last say to your husband or wife, come away with me?

And for the believer, there is a greater spring coming. The winter of this fallen world will end, and the one who loves his church will call her to come away with him into a world made new.

verseByVerse.quote: O my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the crannies of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet, and your face is lovely.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the crannies of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet, and your face is lovely.

She is like a dove hiding in a rock crevice, shy, out of reach. Perhaps she is still hesitant to come out. He does not drag her out. He tells her what he wants: let me see your face, let me hear your voice. And he tells her why: your voice is sweet, your face is lovely.

Some people hide from those who love them, afraid to be seen or heard. Love coaxes them out with gentleness and assurance. That is also how the Lord deals with timid hearts. He wants to hear your voice in prayer, not because he needs information, but because he delights in you.

verseByVerse.quote: Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that spoil the vineyards, for our vineyards are in blossom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that spoil the vineyards, for our vineyards are in blossom."

The ESV notes that the animals may be jackals. Either way, small animals got into vineyards in spring and destroyed the tender blossoms before the grapes could form. The love of the couple is like a vineyard in blossom, and it needs protecting.

It is seldom the great disasters that destroy a marriage. It is the little foxes: the unkind word left unapologised for, the screen that takes the evening, the small resentments, the busyness, the neglect. Catch the foxes for us: it is a shared job. Name the little foxes in your own marriage, or friendship, or walk with God, and catch them before they spoil the fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved is mine, and I am his; he grazes among the lilies. Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, turn, my beloved, be like a gazelle or a young stag on cleft mountains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My beloved is mine, and I am his; he grazes among the lilies.

Here is the heart of the Song in a single line. My beloved is mine, and I am his. Mutual belonging. Not ownership in the sense of control, but the covenant belonging of marriage, where each gives himself to the other. The ESV notes that he grazes may be rendered "he pastures his flock": he is still the shepherd, among the lilies.

The line will return, reversed, I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine (6:3), and again, I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me (7:10). Notice the movement: first she speaks of possessing him, then of belonging to him, and finally of resting in his desire for her. Love matures from "he is mine" to "I am his".

That is the movement of faith too. The believer begins by rejoicing that Christ is his. He grows into the deeper joy that he belongs to Christ. I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14).

Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, turn, my beloved, be like a gazelle or a young stag on cleft mountains.

Until the morning breeze comes and the night shadows go, she asks him to come to her, swift as a gazelle over the mountains. The ESV notes that cleft mountains may be rendered "mountains of Bether". The chapter ends with longing for him to be near through the night.

2.title: My Beloved Is Mine, and I Am His
2.overview:
The bride calls herself a common wildflower, and her beloved calls her a lily among brambles; she calls him an apple tree among forest trees, and delights in his shade and fruit (vv. 1-3). He brings her to the banqueting house, and his banner over her is love; faint with love, she rests in his embrace (vv. 4-6). She charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it pleases (v. 7).

Her beloved comes leaping over the hills and calls through the lattice, Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away, for winter is past and spring has come (vv. 8-13). He longs to see her face and hear her voice (v. 14) and asks that the little foxes that spoil the vineyards be caught (v. 15). My beloved is mine, and I am his (vv. 16-17).
2.theology:
Married love is a protecting, public and delighting love (vv. 3-4), and its physical expression is good (v. 6; Heb 13:4). Desire must not be awakened before its time; sexual purity is God's will (v. 7; 1 Thess 4:3-5).

Love must be guarded against small threats (v. 15). Husband and wife belong to each other in covenant (v. 16; 1 Cor 7:4). Christ's love is a banner over his people (v. 4; Rom 5:8); he comes and calls rather than forces (vv. 8-9; Rev 3:20), and his people belong to him (John 10:14).
2.examples:
A crocus among thousands on the plain.

A banner that tells everyone whose you are.

A fire in the hearth, and a fire loose in the house.

A face at the lattice, and a voice calling come away.

The screen that takes the evening: a little fox.
